beats.say: Somewhere there is an orchard. And in it, one number we will never see exactly: the average weight of all its oranges.
Statistics is the art of saying something true about that number, using only a handful of oranges.
This film walks through how a frequentist does it, chapter by chapter, and why every step is there.
We begin at a pool table, with a thought experiment from an essay of Thomas Bayes, published in seventeen sixty-three.
A white ball comes to rest at some unknown height. Then red balls are rolled, and for each one we learn a single fact: did it stop below the white ball, or above it?
From those reports alone: where is the white ball?
A Bayesian treats its position as uncertain, and spreads belief across the table. A curve that sharpens with every ball.
A frequentist refuses. The white ball is somewhere, fixed. What is random are the balls. So the frequentist asks a different question: if I repeated this experiment, how would my estimate behave?
That question, how would my method behave over repetitions, is the heart of frequentist statistics. The rest of this film unpacks it.
Now, the orchard. Mew, the true average weight, plays the white ball: fixed, hidden, the thing we want.
The oranges we pick play the red balls. We weigh ten of them. On average, one hundred and thirty-nine grams.
Pick a different ten, and every number changes. The truth stays put. The sample moves.
So a frequentist never says, mew is probably below one hundred and fifty grams. Every probability they state describes the method, never the truth itself.
What does probability mean, then? For a frequentist, it is a long-run frequency.
Repeat the experiment many times, and count how often an event happens. Say, the average of ten oranges falling below one hundred and forty grams.
Early on, the ratio jumps around. Over thousands of repetitions, it settles. Here, at about fourteen and a half percent.
The cloud of averages from all those imagined repetitions has a name: the sampling distribution. Every tool that follows is a statement about it.
To know that distribution without endless repetition, we make four assumptions.
The target is fixed. The oranges are picked at random. The orchard does not change while we look.
And the average behaves like a bell curve.
That last one is a gift of the central limit theorem. Even when single oranges are lopsided, averages of many become bell-shaped.
But notice which failures hurt. A lopsided orchard bends the guarantees a little. Picking only the oranges near the road breaks them completely, and more oranges will not help.
Our one hundred and thirty-nine grams is an estimate: one draw from the distribution of all possible averages.
Two facts describe that distribution. Its centre is the truth. The average does not systematically miss.
And its spread, sigma over the square root of n, is the standard error. Errors in independent oranges partly cancel, so averages wobble far less than single oranges.
Four times the oranges halves the wobble.

To estimate sigma itself, we divide by n minus one, not n. The sample average sits closer to its own data than the truth does, so the deviations come out slightly too small. By exactly one orange's worth.
Now the central move. Our average missed the grower's one hundred and fifty grams by eleven. Is that a lot?
It depends on the oranges. So we stop measuring in grams, and measure in standard errors instead. Our miss is two point three three of them.
Measured this way, the miss follows one universal curve, whatever the orchard's average, and whatever its spread. The units cancel. Statisticians call such a quantity a pivot.
Because our ruler is itself estimated, the curve has slightly heavier tails: Student's t. Its middle ninety-five percent is fenced at plus or minus two point two six two.
The first decision tool is the hypothesis test. Assume the grower is right, and ask: would our data be surprising?
If the true average were one hundred and fifty grams, a sample as low as ours, or lower, turns up only two point two percent of the time. That is the p value.
It falls below our threshold of five percent, fixed in advance. So we reject the claim.

But be precise. The p value is not the chance that the grower is right. And failing to reject would not have proved him right: with ten oranges, this test misses a real five gram shortfall three times out of four.
The second tool turns the question around. Instead of testing one value, collect every value the data cannot rule out.
Our ninety-five percent confidence interval runs from one hundred and twenty-eight point three, to one hundred and forty-nine point seven grams.
Here is the subtle part. The truth is either inside it, or not. There is no probability left.
The ninety-five percent describes the method. Like a player who rings the peg nineteen times in twenty, it describes the skill, never a single ring.
Those guarantees come with a condition: you must follow the plan.
Imagine an impatient inspector, who tests after every single orange, and stops the moment the p value dips below five percent.
Every grower she inspects is honest. Yet the p value wanders, and each peek is another lottery ticket. Instead of five percent, she accuses nearly a third of them.
Same data, different procedure, different error rate. The guarantee belongs to the rule, not to the numbers on the page.
Step back, and the whole method fits on one line.
Treat the truth as fixed. Model how the data arise. Choose an estimator.
Imagine repeating the experiment. Turn the miss into a pivot.
Then test, or build an interval. And decide, knowing how often you would be wrong.
We can never see the white ball. We can never weigh every orange.
But we can know, precisely and honestly, how often our methods lead us astray.
That is the quiet power of frequentist reasoning. Not certainty about the truth, but certainty about ourselves.
